a reference to an apology following a statement made at a hearing of the Waitangi
Tribunal amongst the Ngāpuhi people. We heard the statements made by a former
member of this Committee, Dover Samuels. He said to the tribunal that it is only right
that the Crown apologise to him and those of his generation.
But we of New Zealand First do not act ually support that view. And why not? In the
time of Sir Apirana Ngata, he and an associate exhorted Māori to equip themselves for
the material world of the Pākehā. As part of the preparation, the children of the time
had to learn to speak English, along w ith other skills. That was appropriate for those
times because the majority of Māori had but one language, the Māori language. In the
light of that, we of New Zealand First do not think it right to call on the Crown to
apologise for the actions of a great leader of the time. So what now? What fellow
colleague Nanaia asserted is correct: we, the Māori Affairs Committee members,
considered this matter and decided to refer it the Committee for consideration. That is
the reason we are addressing that situation at this point in time. So that is our view on
that matter.
We heard the comments about the Te Mātāwai group, and at the time of my last
address when this bill was in the House, I said to the Minister that we opposed a hapū
register. It is not right that so  many tribes be crammed into five, four, or even three
regions. I know this and so do you, Minister.
Last week I also attended a meeting in the far north to speak on this matter about
selecting a representative for the far north. The outcome was to delete the tribal names
and and leave it as the far north region, and for the tribes in attendance at that meeting
to select a representative for the region, as not all subtribes and tribes attended that
meeting. If you don’t see your subtribe on the register, th en it might have been
overlooked. That was the thinking of that meeting; that was the reasoning to dispense
with those names. Leave it for that meeting to satisfy their wishes.
So, Minister, despite the trials and tribulations in introducing this bill, we continue
to commend you.

items.speaker: Hon Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Are you saying you support it?

items.speaker: PITA PARAONE
items.text: No! Not at all, because there are many parts in it that we do not
support, like some groups that supported you in the past, because I received a letter
10226 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 05 Apr 2016
from Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i Te Reo that you are aware of, Minister, expressing some
concern of theirs. We of New Zealand First have a perception that they may have
traversed a righteous path to oppose some statements in the bill. B ut at the end of the
day we acknowledge your efforts, Minister. The bill has undergone many changes since
the one your predecessor, Pita, introduced into the House.
In conclusion, I laugh to myself and say: what is the purpose of the bill? To make
people p roficient in our chiefly language? But why am I amused? For this one is
standing here and, although not very proficient in our language, giving effect to it and
opposing its function. So what can be done about it? But the main thing is that this bill
has e merged, and we and the nation are hearing our chiefly language tonight. So
acknowledgments and congratulations once again to you, and to us collectively, thank
you.]

TUESDAY, 5 APRIL 2016 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
United States—Delegation, House of Representatives 
Mr SPEAKER: I am sure that members would wish to welcome Congressman Matt 
Salmond and Congresswoman Cynthia Lummis of the United States House of 
Representatives, present in the gallery. 
MOTIONS 
United Nations, Secretary-General—Nomination of Rt Hon Helen Clark 
ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Op position): I seek leave to move a motion 
without notice or debate on the nomination of the Rt Hon Helen Clark for the position 
of Secretary-General of the United Nations. 
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objec tion? 
There is none. 
ANDREW LITTLE : I move, That this House express its support for the Rt Hon 
Helen Clark’s announcement that she will stand for the UN Secretary -General role this 
year. I note that she has been an exceptional head of the U N Development Programme 
and brings her experience as a leader of a country, and that she is, and always has been, 
a trailblazer, following a long line of Kiwi women who have broken through the glass 
ceiling. 
Motion agreed to. 
POINTS OF ORDER 
Chamber—Visual Aids 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip —Labour): I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. 
Last week in the House we had some interchange arou nd the use of visual aids by 
members in which you indicated that a visual aid could not be held up by a member 
sitting next to another member. I want to draw your attention, having had the chance to 
consider it now, to Speaker’s ruling 64/1, which was a ru ling from 2010 by Speaker 
Smith in which he indicated that although it was not acceptable for members in general 
to be holding up visual aids, it was acceptable for a member sitting next to a member 
speaking to be holding up a visual aid that they were ref erring to during their 
contribution. I just want to seek some reassurance from you that in fact that Speaker’s 
ruling does still apply and that there is not going to be a change in that practice. 
Mr SPEAKER : Yes, I have given c onsiderable thought to this matter since last 
week, and I think the ruling by Speaker Smith is eminently sensible. It seems to be that 
when a member is concentrating on the question, then it is absolutely appropriate that a 
bench mate be allowed to assist with the holding of a visual aid. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Tax System—Overseas Trusts 
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: How 
does he stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): On foot. [Interruption]  
10140 Oral Questions 5 Apr 2016 
 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! [ Interruption] Order! We now need to get to the serious 
business of question time with substantially less interjection from quite a number of 
prominent people in the House. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : How can he stand by his statements yesterday that New 
Zealand “is not a tax haven” and that we “also have an extensive disclosure regime”, 
when specialist law firms on trusts for foreigners point out there is no need for 
disclosure of identity, or trust registration, or for any such trust accounts to be audited? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Because I am right. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: This is now the third time I have asked for a little bit of cooperation, 
and I am going to have to expect it in the future. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : How can he argue that he is right and that our legal 
requirements and obligations are both transparent and require disclosure when the 
Inland Revenue Department is not required to share information with foreign 
jurisdictions unless that jurisdiction suspects offending and then asks it for information? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Because I am correct and the member is wrong. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am not saying that I 
am right. I am asking him a simple question that does n ot require that flippant answer, 
now twice. 
Mr SPEAKER: No, the question started with “How can he argue that he is right” 
and the Prime Minister gave an answer that satisfied that. The member might not agree 
with it but it addressed the question.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Does he agree with John Christensen, the executive 
director of Tax Justice Network, that: “Trusts are used, in many instances, as one of the 
basic building blocks of these sophisticated tax evasion structures.”; if not, why not? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I am not here to be a tax trust expert, but people use trusts for 
all sorts of reasons. They use them because they want to have their assets held because 
they may, for instance, be sued, or they may  use trusts for all sorts of other reasons. 
Members of this House use them all the time. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Quoting from this long statement from the Prime Minister: 
“Tax havens are where there is non -disclosure of information. N ew Zealand has full 
disclosure of information so all you’ve got is a situation where New Zealand has taken a 
different view from a lot of jurisdictions and that’s because the way we tax is we tax a 
settlor, in other words, it’s all about making sure that New Zealanders”— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: —“pay their fair share of tax.” 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I do need a supplementary question, not a long quote. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Well, having to conclude: “it’s all about making sure that 
New Zealanders pay their fair share of tax.” What on earth does that mumbo -jumbo 
really mean? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, it sounded a lot better when I said it, but the answer was 
that we tax a settlor, and the reason we tax settlors is that it is good tax policy. It stops 
New Zealanders actually creating taxes in all sorts of foreign jurisdictions and avoiding 
paying tax in their home country called New Zealand. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: If he is right, why are so many international commentators, 
and now the Australians, having a go at us for being, in their words, “a tax haven”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As the member knows, people throw around all sorts o f 
comments, but New Zealand is not a tax haven. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Can he assure this House that none of his present or former 
Ministers—that is, him as Prime Minister —have been and are involved in tax haven 
activity? 
5 Apr 2016 Oral Questions 10141 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I cannot speak for any other member, because we have a 
pecuniary interests list that people have to record, but as I have recorded on my 
pecuniary interests I have two trusts. One of them has been the long -established trust I 
have had in my wife’s name, the JP & BI Key Family Trust, and the other is the Aldgate 
Trust, which was established so it could be a blind trust so that when I became Prime 
Minister all of my assets could go in there. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The Hon Amy Adams, I have called 
for order. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Is that blind trust one with 20/20 vision? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I have no ministerial responsibility there other than to say tha t 
a blind trust was established, as other Prime Ministers have, because it is good practice 
to do so. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Why since he has become the Prime Minister has there 
been a threefold increase in offshore trusts operating in New Zealand, were it not for the 
discovery internationally of just how lax our tax money - laundering disclosure regime 
is? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : That is not true. Tax laws around trusts were established in 
New Zealand in 1988. The disclosu re regime change was implemented in 2006. 
Subsequent to that there have been a number of other things that have been done to 
improve aspects of trusts. In 2013 the OECD gave a report on New Zealand and fully 
cleared New Zealand. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: If that is the case, why, subsequent to that date he gave as 
the reason why we should be all relaxed about it, have the Ministry of Business 
Innovation and Employment and Treasury expressed their concern about the existence 
of tax haven activity in New Zealand, and why should we believe him and not them? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: As I said, in 2013 the OECD gave New Zealand a clean bill of 
health. What has also happened is that New Zealand continues to work with the OECD 
about it s base minimisation, but the Inland Revenue Department regularly puts up a 
menu of options that could be looked at as part of its work programme. It was not the 
No. 1 priority for the Government at the time because, compared with other measures 
where we could have them working, it would actually be about collecting more tax for 
New Zealanders. 
Tax System—Overseas Trusts and Disclosure Regime 
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement that New Zealand is not a tax haven because “New Zealand has 
full disclosure of information”, given Cone Marshall, a law firm specialising in 
establishing trusts for foreigners, says “The identity of t he settlor need not be disclosed 
and the trust deed is not registered with any tax or Government authority” and “There is 
no obligation to file any trust accounts with any person or institution or to have such 
accounts audited”? 
Mr SPEAKER: As I call the right honourable Prime Minister, my office has been 
advised that this answer may well be longer than normal. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, because there is more than on e step in 
the disclosure process. Initially, a New Zealand resident trustee must submit a foreign 
trust disclosure form, an IR607, which simply records the name of the trust and the 
trustee’s contact details. However, the trustee must also keep detailed fi nancial and 
other records, including the trust deed; details of settlements and distributions, including 
the recipient’s name and address; details of the trust’s assets and liabilities; the identities 
of the settlors and the beneficiaries of the trust; and  money that the trust receives and 
spends. The Inland Revenue Department can get this kind of information and will give 
10142 Oral Questions 5 Apr 2016 
 
it to the tax authorities in any other country if requested under a relevant tax agreement, 
or proactively if that country wishes. I am advised by the Inland Revenue Department 
that New Zealand has always been able to comply with these sorts of information 
requests from treaty partners. This is certainly full disclosure of information. The 
income in these trusts is quite rightly outside ou r tax base. It is foreign income earned 
by foreigners. It is up to other tax authorities around the world to enforce their own tax 
laws on this income and on their own residents. We can help them do that by providing 
detailed information to them on request  about trusts that are administered from New 
Zealand. I make the second point, which is that we automatically disclose that 
information to Australia. It is the one jurisdiction that has asked us; no other jurisdiction 
has. These disclosure regimes, which b y any definition are broad and deep, were the 
ones passed by the Labour Government in 2006. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [Interruption] Order! 
Andrew Little : Is he seriously telling the House that the only obligation that a  
foreign trust is obliged to make, which is completion of an IR706 form and nothing else, 
constitutes a full disclosure regime for this type of vehicle? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : For a start off, it is an IR607 form, not an IR706 form. And, 
secondly, as I pointed out in the answer, which was very long and very detailed, that is 
but the starting point, which requires them to keep hugely detailed information of what 
is in there and report that when required. Those are the rules that Labour thought we re 
right when it passed this disclosure in 2006. If the member is now telling us that Labour 
got it wrong, he should get on his feet and apologise. 
Andrew Little: Why has he failed to heed the warnings from the New Zealand Law 
Commission, t he Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand, the OECD, and 
the Inland Revenue Department that New Zealand’s weak offshore tax laws allow 
wealthy foreigners to subvert laws and dodge taxes? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am prepared to accept t hat I made one mistake, and that is 
relying on Labour. It passed the rules. 
Andrew Little: Can he guarantee that no offshore trusts registered in New Zealand 
are being used to hide illegally obtained assets or dodge tax? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No Prime Minister can give that assurance any more than 
Helen Clark could have when this law was passed, no doubt with the support of David 
Parker, in 2006. What is quite clear is that New Zealand gives all of that information not 
only to A ustralia but to any jurisdiction that asks for it. We have been able to comply 
with every jurisdiction that has asked. I also note that we have 40 double tax agreements 
and 11 information-sharing agreements, one of which includes Malta. 
Andrew Little: What effect does he think it has on New Zealand’s reputation when 
we are viewed as a tax haven harbouring billions of dollars, and his only reaction is to 
boast that it earns us $24 million a year in lawyers’ fees and accountants’ fees? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : New Zealand is not a tax haven. Tax havens do not have the 
disclosure regimes that New Zealand has. It is as simple as this: if it is such a bad idea, 
it was Labour in 1988 that passed the trust legislation, it was Labour in 2006 that had— 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: Point of order. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: —the disclosure— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [ Interruption] Order! When I rise to my feet, it requires the 
Prime Minister to cease his answer. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. For countless answers 
now the Prime Minister has departed from doing his job of answering the question, and 
attacked another political party for a law that is 10 years old, and 7 years after he got the 
job. Please ask him to act responsibly and answer the questions he is being asked. 
5 Apr 2016 Oral Questions 10143 
 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! The Prime Minister addressed the question almost 
immediately, and then, because he was then responding to interje ctions, which were 
not—[Interruption] Order! Because the Prime Minister was then responding to 
interjections, it is inevitable that some politics will enter into the argument. 
Andrew Little : How does he expect to go to international forums and stop 
multinational corporations dodging their New Zealand tax, when he is letting foreign 
tax-dodgers use New Zealand as a tax haven? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Firstly, I believe the latter part of the question from the 
member to be wrong. Sec ondly, in all of the international forums that I have been in, in 
the nearly 8 years that I have been Prime Minister, no one has ever raised this issue with 
me. I am not aware of them ever raising it with a Minister of Revenue, and, as I said in 
2013, New Zealand was given a clean bill of health by the OECD. 
James Shaw : Does he acknowledge that the Inland Revenue Department said in 
2013 that “our foreign trust rules continue to attract criticism, including claims that New 
Zealand is now a tax haven in respect of trusts.”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I have not seen the particular quote, but, as I said earlier, the 
Inland Revenue Department has come up with a whole range of things it wants on the 
work programme, and I would have thought th e most important thing was making sure 
that New Zealanders actually pay their fair share of tax, and that has been the priority. 
James Shaw : Is he disagreeing with Inland Revenue Department’s advice in 2013 
that the way forward is to strengthe n our disclosure and reporting requirements with 
New Zealand foreign trusts? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: What the Government is doing is working with the OECD on 
its base erosion programmes. It is quite happy to take advice and suggestions from 
others and, over time, there may be arguments about things we could strengthen. But if 
you look at what the requirements are under IR607, they are extremely broad and deep. 
James Shaw : So is he opposed to greater transparency for New Zealand forei gn 
trusts, when greater transparency will only hurt people using foreign trusts for 
illegitimate purposes? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Clearly not, because we have the ultimate in disclosure when 
it comes to Australia, because we give it full disclo sure without even making reference 
to the Australians, because they ask for it. We would do it for any other jurisdiction that 
asked us to do that. If any country wants to come to New Zealand and have the same 
requirements as Australia has asked us for, we  will provide it with all that information. 
As I said in my answer to the primary question, which was quite long, New Zealand 
actually collates a great deal of information and it shares it with every jurisdiction that 
asks us. 
James Shaw: So would the Prime Minister agree with me that for foreign trusts with 
nothing to hide, they should have nothing to fear from greater transparency?

DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First): I first of all want to refer to clause 8, which is the 
one that provides for the mixed elected and appointed council —seven elected and six 
appointed—and I just want to say this. I think that is a risky kind of a council to 
establish. It is likely to create tensio ns between those who are appointed and those who 
are elected. We are likely to get a them-and-us attitude, and it is not going to be positive 
for an organisation that should actually be representative of the people and not of the 
Government. So I will leav e that there. I have said that I think it is a bad idea. I have 
said that it is likely to be dysfunctional, and I think it will be.  
I want to go on and say this about clause 8(1)(a). In the first version of the bill it 
referred to only “7 elected members;”, but now it refers to “no fewer than 4 and no more 
than 7 elected members;”. So it is envisaged that there will be, in some circumstances, 
fewer than seven elected members at a particular time, although under clause 8(1)(b) 
there will be up to six appoin ted members and there could, therefore, be at any 
particular time a majority, in fact, of appointed people and not of elected people. I 
presume the reason why this clause has been drafted in the way it is is that it would 
provide for deaths or resignations  of elected people, and that is fair enough. But why is 
it not drafted to preserve the majority of elected people over appointed people at all 
times?  
The Ministers could suspend any particular appointed person or persons in order to 
maintain a majority of  elected people, and that is what should have been done in the 
bill. Otherwise, the Government, and the Ministers, are accepting the possibility —in 
fact, almost the inevitability —that there could be, at a particular time, a majority of 
appointed people ove r elected ones, because many councils have either deaths or 
resignations for some reason or another during a 3 -year term. So I think that is a 
problem in the bill that simply has not been addressed, and perhaps the Minister in the 
chair would like to comment on that.  
I want to move on, however, to the reference in clause 11(2), which deals with 
appointed members and the need for skills. It seems to me that this is one of the main 
reasons why the Government believes that there needs to actually be appointed

I also want to talk about subclause (1A), which relates to Ngāi Tahu representation. 
This is where we in New Zealand First depart from all of the other parties in the 
Committee. We think that having Ngāi Tahu representation, especially as many as two 
members, on Environment Canterbury is wrong in principle. We think that having any 
appointed members is wrong in principle. We think, quite apart from that, that the

Tahu people, the views of whom, for example, must be taken particular notice of by 
Environment Canterbury in making its decisions. But actual membership by 
appointment to an elected body is wrong, and New Zealand First would definitely 
always oppose that. We know that other parties do not have that position, but we do.  
For all of those reasons, I would say that this bill should not be passed. But, again, I

said why, really, when in fact that is not in the bill at all. What is in the bill is the need

regard to all of that, we actually need appointed members at all. Why not just go straight

The CHAIRPERSON (Hon Chester Borrows) : Before we commence de bate on 
this bill, there are several procedural matters that I want to comment on. Firstly, the title 
and commencement clauses of this bill are contained in Part 1AA. The debate on this 
part will be taken first, and there will be no concluding title and co mmencement clause 
debate. The second matter relates to the dual -language nature of the bill. As you will be 
aware, the Te Reo Māori and English texts of this bill have equal authority. Neither text 
10206 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 05 Apr 2016 
 
is to be considered a translation of the other, though the y are intended to be equivalent 
in meaning. I will recognise this in the conducting of the Committee’s consideration of 
the bill. For the purposes of debate, the Te Reo Māori and English text for each part will 
be taken together. Hence, the question for th e first part will be that Te Wāhanga tahi 
AA—that is, Part 1AA—and that Part 1AA stand part. 
I note that separate amendments to the two texts are possible. The Minister’s 
Supplementary Order Paper 164 amends Te Reo Māori text for Part 1AA but does not 
amend the English text, as there are matters requiring amendment in one but not the 
other. Recognising that the two texts are separate, the votes on the two texts will be 
taken separately. 
Further, because the two texts of the bill are of equal authority, amen dments that are 
in one language are not automatically treated as amending the other text of the bill. If a 
substantive amendment is to be agreed to by the Committee, it is highly desirable that 
the text in both Te Reo Māori and English is agreed to. If it appears likely that the 
amendment that is proposed in only one language is not to be agreed to by the 
Committee, the Minister may wish to postpone further consideration of the part under 
Standing Order 303(1)(d) and (4), to allow time for the amendment to be drafted in the 
other language. For that further amendment to be tabled, the alternative is to have a bill 
that may be deficient in one of the language versions.

a guardianship responsibility for the language, and to guide Māori language - related 
issues; the Te Mātāwai entity will be accordingly established. Its task will be to give

treated accordingly. This bill in no way changes its unique status in the nation, which

[Greetings, Mr Chairman, and all gathered here this evening on this matter. First, I 
lament the passing of my elder kin Whairiri Ngata, who lies in state in Ngati Porou 
territory in the realm of his hapū, Te Aitanga -a-Mate, in the porch of his ancestral 
house Kapohanga on Hiruhārama Marae. I am desolate that I was unable to attend his 
funeral. At this moment I think of my great -aunt Mihihara. She is almost 90 years of 
age, her son Whairiri lying in state on the porch. It is only proper that we farewell his 
passing, Minister Flavell, he and others lying in state on many marae throughout the 
land. So farewell to all our losses. 
Returning now to the gathering here this evening, we the living embodiment of the 
dead, we who are gathered here to discuss this great matter pertaining to our language 
and the dialects of individual iwi, the beauty of the  various dialects of Aotearoa. It is 
only right that we honour the memory of Whairiri and his father, Hōri Mahue, for they, 
allied with others, compiled a dictionary of the Māori language for all our benefit. 
Tonight our debate focuses on the treasure that  is our Māori language, the 
indigenous language of this country. This bill, however, does not give effect to the 
prestige of the language in the annals of the law, lest we have the mistaken belief that is 
the process we are going through, for the language has its own innate prestige. The 
focus of our discussions this evening is a language for all of Aotearoa. The member 
from the Opposition is correct; all people will find their interests accommodated within 
this bill. If that is our goal, to ensure the survival and the maturation of our language so 
that all the people of Aotearoa are conversant with the language, the songs, the chants, 
and haka entirely in our language, this bill before us is one of great importance. It is a 
foundation for the language. 
The bill sets out the role of iwi and Māori communities and the role of the Crown. 
Let me clarify. The Crown is not limited to members sitting on this side of the Chamber. 
Rather, the Crown is represented by all the members of this Committee. Therefore, we 
all have a responsibility to carry out the provisions of this bill, regardless of who is the 
Government of the time, regardless of the wrongs of individual Governments. But the 
challenge before us this evening is to revitalise our language, whether in the edu cation 
10214 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 05 Apr 2016 
 
system or otherwise. I fully support that and language initiatives in our tertiary 
institutions, but the main focus of our efforts should be to return the language as a 
language of common use in the home, on the sports fields, in our places of relig ion, and 
when we go to the shops. All places should be places where the language can be, and is, 
spoken. If we succeed in those contexts we will have come a long way to ensuring the 
language will be alive for our generations growing and generations yet bor n. It is a 
treasure. The beauty of this treasure is that it accommodates the dialects of individual 
iwi. That is a beautiful thing to adorn our country. 
The strategy for iwi and Māori communities will be formulated by iwi and the Māori 
community. That is the challenge to them and that is the challenge to the members of 
this Committee and Government. And we must formulate an effective strategy that 
encapsulates all Government agencies, a strategy that enhances and supports the 
dreams and aspirations of iwi and Māori. I support this. This will not be an easy task 
for the group Te Mātāwai. Another challenge will be the composition of Te Mātāwai. It 
must represent the interests of all people, of all iwi, of all hapū, of all marae. It will be a 
difficult task to choose the membership of that panel, for, as we know, despite their 
achievements they will not be able to realise all our aspirations. So I urge us, do n ot 
leave this work of great moment just in the hands of Te Mātāwai or the Government or 
the Crown. We must exhort each other to speak the Māori language. 
As you listen to my speech you can pick up errors of a grammatical nature; some of 
my words are not quite the right fit. However, if we do not make an attempt to speak, the 
language will not survive. So I urge us all to speak, regardless. I recall when my mother 
was alive. She was a true Ngati. Every day that would dawn, she would speak our Ngati 
Porou dialect and at day’s end she would be speaking the dialect of Ngati Porou. She 
would listen to me speaking on television or on the radio, then ring me up to berate me: 
“You did not say this correctly, you said that wrongly, but keep talking our language.” 
That is the strength and value of our parents, of our mothers. No matter if the language 
be Māori or English or some other, we must strive to improve our proficiency. 
That is the sum of my contribution this evening, and I applaud the Minister for Māori 
Development. This has been a trying time for you, your predecessor Pita, and the Māori 
Party. I salute you, the chairman of the Māori Affairs Committee, Nuk Korako, for the 
rigour that your select committee put this bill through. Commendations to us this 
evening on this marvellous bill that aims to ensure the survival and retention of our 
language for the generations to come. Acknowledgments to us all, and thank you.]

One of the principles in the bill talks about sustaining Te Reo Māori and how that 
can be done intergenerationally. My concern is that we may not be actually addressing 
that particular issue in a way that includes those generations that have missed out on 
having Te Reo Māori as their mother language, including myself.  
I want to say this in English, that the historical and intergenerational trauma caused 
by Government policy of the day has meant th at the language was virtually lost over 
less than three generations. My overall concern is whether or not the measures taken in 
this bill will be enough. But I do endorse the words from the Hon Hekia Parata and 
what she contributed to the Committee.  
We actually cannot rely on just the Government and the Crown alone. We have to, as 
Māori, whānau, hapū, and iwi, also take that responsibility. My hope, in this bill, is that 
through having a Māori strategy and a Crown strategy we will indeed be able to help the 
situation that most of a whole generation or two have found themselves in, and that the 
decline in speaking Te Reo Māori, from 25 percent in 2001 down to 21.13 percent in 
2013, can be halted and turned round, to the point that we can get to a sustainable  level. 
I understand it is mostly accepted that you need to have 30 percent of your population 
being able to speak the language for it to be sustainable. Nō reira, koinā aku whakaaro i 
te tuata’i, e Te Komiti tēnā tātau.

Mr Chair, thank you for the opportunity to speak on Part 1 of this bill. I will briefly 
work through clauses 3 to 10 that make up t his part. Firstly, I wish to talk about the 
scope and purpose of this bill. And that is to emphasise the status of the Māori language 
as the indigenous language of New Zealand, as a taonga of iwi and Māori, as a 
language valued by the nation, and as the official language of New Zealand. It is to that 
very important purpose that the next three clauses give effect. One element of clause 4 
is an amendment added by the Māori Affairs Committe to clarify that declaring iwi and 
Māori as the guardians of the Māori language does not limit or somehow reduce the 
responsibilities of the Crown. While this bill gives more of the responsibilities of 
guardianship of the language to iwi, it does not absolve the Crown of its 
responsibilities, and the addition of clause 4(3) ensures that it does not. 
The Minister for Māori Development’s Supplementary Order Paper 164 introduces a 
new clause here, clause 5A. This clause is an acknowledgment clause, similar in vein to 
the acknowledgments contained in Treaty settlement bills. It ac knowledges the past 
wrongs of the Crown in failing to protect and promote the Māori language, and its 
commitment to work in partnership with iwi and Māori to protect the language in the 
future. This is a very important clause and one which I am very glad t o see included in 
the bill. The bill is about the future, and takes the Māori language in the state it is now 
and charts a way of moving forward with the strengthening of the language. But it is 
important that the bill begins by acknowledging past injustic es and acknowledging that 
in the past the Crown has got it wrong. With this clause added to the bill, we can move 
into the principles that will guide the bill and the provisions that will provide the 
practical means to support and revitalise the Māori language. 
Clause 6 is largely a continuation of the right to speak Māori in legal proceedings 
that was already affirmed under the Māori Language Act 1987. Clause 6A sets out the 
principles that will guide the interpretation of this Act and the development of M āori 
language strategies under it. I have already touched on the importance of the Crown 
continuing to have a responsibility to promote and support the Māori language in 
future. These responsibilities are further expanded on by the principles clause. There  is 
one phrase that is particularly important, and that is “active partnership”. The Crown 
is to be an active partner with iwi and Māori. When this bill is passed, Te Mātāwai will 
be established.  
However, the Crown’s work continues; it does not end there.  Both sides must work 
on to promote the language. Clause 7 gives some guiding principles for departments of 
State. These include the need to consult with iwi and Māori on matters related to 
language retention, and the need to use the Māori language in the promotion of 
Government services and information to the public. The next two clauses, 7A and 7B, 
set out the two parallel strategies that will be developed under this bill. These dual 
strategies once again highlight the thread running through this bill: th at promotion, 
10218 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 05 Apr 2016 
 
protection, and revitalisation of the Māori language is not only a Crown responsibility 
or the responsibility of the iwi and Māori; it is a shared responsibility. The two 
strategies will set out the objectives, policies, and related matters f or the Crown and Te 
Mātāwai respectively in relation to the language. 
Clause 7C highlights the ground -breaking nature of this bill. This is the second bill 
to contain the full text in both Māori and English, but it is the first bill where the Māori 
text will take precedence should a conflict in the meaning between the two versions ever 
arise. We hope that situation never arises, and we have a robust translation that is clear 
and not prone to differences of interpretation. However, if that situation ever doe s arise 
before the court, it is appropriate that, in this bill, the Māori language version takes 
precedence. 
The rest of Part 1 is administrative, and includes an outline of the Act. Part 1 of the 
bill sets out the importance of cooperation between the Cro wn and Māori, through Te 
Mātāwai. It affirms the status of Māori in New Zealand Government and society, and 
sets the stage for the remaining parts of the bill. Therefore, Mr Chair, I acknowledge 
you and everyone in this Chamber; my greetings and salutations to you all.]

Higgins is the chairperson, and the membership compr ises Ruakere Hond, Dr 
Wharehuia Milroy, Charisma Rangipunga, and Charlie Te Pana. Congratulations on 
this great piece of work, maintaining consistency with the aims set forth by the Minister 
10220 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 05 Apr 2016 
 
for Māori Development while giving credence to the views of the M āori people, and we 
see the fruits of that effort in this bill before us this evening. 
And this is but the beginning. You are correct, and we of the select committee 
concur, that the Māori language has primacy over the English language in this piece of 
legislation. We asked what would happen if this legislation was taken before the courts. 
The response of your officials was that the Māori language version would retain 
primacy within Māori court settings “and that is a good thing”, hence the title of this 
bill, Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill. I fully support the primacy of the 
Māori language in the title of this bill. There are two clauses in Part 1AA. One clause 
concerns the title, and I have expressed my views on that; another clause concerns  the 
commencement of the bill. It is good that on the completion of our debate we can enact 
the bill in its entirety. 
As for this group Te Pūtahi Pāoho, I am strongly of the view that it should be done 
away with. I agree with the deadline given for its dis establishment, 30 March next year. 
That is a good thing. When I think of that group and its past work, the time has come to 
disestablish it, and I support that. 
Let me focus on the discussions of the Māori Affairs Committee regarding the main 
pillars of this bill. We agree with the dual strategies approach, a Māori strategy and a 
Crown strategy, but the challenge is to mesh the two strategies to give effect to the 
revitalisation of the language. We would appreciate a steer from you, Minister, as to 
how you see this working. 
Secondly, the apology by the Crown. This was discussed by the select committee. I 
asked that the select committee unanimously agree that an apology be included in the 
bill. It is an easy thing to write into the bill. However, the select c ommittee could not 
reach unanimity on this matter. That is why, Minister, we have brought the matter to the 
Committee of the whole House for all the parties to glean the wishes of the Crown 
either way. It would be a good thing if all parties would agree to  include an apology in 
the bill: set out the history, the original school system, native schools, and the past 
policies of the Crown to suppress us. I recall the stories I heard at home, the stories 
from my uncles and aunties about their experiences attend ing school. Their memories 
are still vivid of those times, the negative experiences. 
That is why I consider this bill a fresh starting point, a new beginning, a path 
forward while holding on to the memories of those hard times, the experiences of our 
elders who strove to retain the language within the whānau, despite the negative 
experiences of the school system. Through their efforts the language still survives, albeit 
only just, on our marae and within our whānau. You are well acquainted with my level 
of language proficiency. In my own whānau, I recall the elders who offered me 
guidance. The main thing they taught me was to think as a Māori, to speak only good, 
and in time your words will truly express your thoughts. Unto this day I still cleave unto 
those teachings. 
So congratulations, Minister. And let me thank our chairperson, Nuk. He is 
accomplished in allowing free discourse by members of the select committee on all 
matters. He broke matters down to their constituent parts; this allowed free and frank 
debate on all aspects of this bill, indeed all bills that come before the select committee. I 
also considered the role of your officials. It is a difficult task for the officials to balance 
their responsibilities to the select committee and their responsib iilties to your expert 
advisory panel. That was an onerous part of their work, and perhaps in the future we 
can look to mitigate that tension. This is not a critique of you, Minister; rather, it is the 
view of the select committee. 
The concluding matter pe rtains to the status of the Māori language. We asked if 
challenges could be made to this bill in court without an appropriate judge—besides the 
05 Apr 2016 Te Pire mō Te Reo Māori / Māori Language Bill 10221 
 
Māori land court judges, besides Justice Joe Williams —a judge able to adjudicate on 
aspects of this bill. Perhap s this is a challenge to increase the numbers of Māori -
speaking judges in the system. Thank you.]

[Thank you, fellow members. I realise you are wanting to speak. However, I am just 
concerned there may be no opportunity to respond to some of the issues raised this 
evening; therefore in this short opportunity I will address directly the points raised. 
First, the point was made in Supplementary Order Paper 166 regarding the balance 
of composition of male and female membership of Te M ātāwai. The problem in the bill, 
however, which will no doubt be mentioned shortly, is that it will be for each region to 
select their own single representative. How can the proportional balance of male and 
female mem bers of the Te Mātāwai entity be achieved if it is up to the arbitrary 
discretion of each region? This is perhaps one response to that issue. However, the 
point has been made that women should have a role in Te Mātāwai. 
Second, the issue of the need to inc rease numbers of speakers of the Māori language 
has been raised, and there is no argument there; that is indeed correct. The problem, 
however, is how to achieve that. The demographic statistics of Māori language speakers 
only appear following the census, w hich means a 4 -yearly review cycle. If the question 
were to be asked “What is the total number of speakers of Māori today?”, the response 
would be a percentage rather than an actual number of speakers. Despite being 
problematic, the goal to increase the nu mber of speakers of the Māori language is 
inescapable. As for the nature of Te Mātāwai, this has already been discussed and I will 
leave it at that for the remainder of this debate. 
Returning to the contribution from the member for Te Tai Hauāuru, to you, Adrian, 
regarding the Māori strategy and the Crown strategy: which will take precedence? In 
short, neither will, although Te Rūnanga Reo forum will be established to support both, 
and will be the centre ridgepole of the framework. Te Rūnanga Reo is the bri nging 
together of both Government Ministers and members of Te Mātāwai to be seated 
together at the planning table for Māori language. That being so, what you have said is 
correct: everyone has a role to play. Our language will not survive by strategy alone . 
As Mārama stated, only by speaking the Māori language will the language survive. 
Returning to the contribution from the member for Canterbury and of the region of 
Ngāi Tahu, what he said cannot be refuted. He adhered to the agenda and, furthermore, 
one good thing mentioned is that this bill has been brought together as a consequence 
of listening to advisory group submissions across the country as my expert advisory 
group undertook its travels, thirdly, all the assistance from the many hands of 
Parliament, and fourthly, but not least, from my department. Therefore, this is the 
embodiment of all that effort and deliberation—another direct benefit of this bill.  
As for the Māori Television Electoral College, enough said. The point has been made 
and I will not  belabour it. For the issue of an apology, I have already shared my view. 
What you have said is correct regarding the pain and the suppression of our language, 
as has been well documented in history books. Those issues still exist and I do feel, yes, 
that what transpired should be acknowledged. However, we need to focus on the 
horizon, looking forward, to be able to say that the survival of our language is in our 
children and grandchildren. 
In conclusion, and so that I can say I have responded to the issues  raised, or at least 
some of them, I commend the statement by the Green Party spokesperson: “Only by 
speaking the language will our language survive into the future.” Thank you, everyone.]

nei. Nā reira, kia ahatia? Ēngari, ko te mea nui kua puta mai te pire nei, kei te ro ngo i a 
tātou, i te motu hoki i tō tātou Reo Rangatira i te pō nei. Nā reira, tēnā koutou, tēnā 
koutou, kia ora mai anō tātou. 
[Greetings, Mr Chairman. I stand on behalf of New Zealand First to address matters 
relating to this bill. Before going on, I add my condolences to those of the Minister for 
Māori Development and others who spoke before me for those who are lost from sight: 
Whai Ngata; Waka Palmer, a pillar of the Rātana faith; and one other mentioned by 
our colleague from Christchurch. It is fitting  because in according tributes to them in 
this situation the beauty of our language comes to the fore. So to you, the dead, depart, 
farewell. 
And so I come back to us, the living; acknowledgments, greetings, and salutations to 
you collectively. My understa nding is that the section we are addressing relates to the 
first part of the bill. Featuring in this part of the bill is an aspect that focuses on the 
apology the Minister proposes to include in this bill. I think to myself, why leave it until 
until now, a nd not when the bill was drafted? My view is that if we wanted to see this 
situation, that was the time to do it. Why now? My conjecture to us is that we are seeing 
a reference to an apology following a statement made at a hearing of the Waitangi 
Tribunal amongst the Ngāpuhi people. We heard the statements made by a former 
member of this Committee, Dover Samuels. He said to the tribunal that it is only right 
that the Crown apologise to him and those of his generation.  
But we of New Zealand First do not act ually support that view. And why not? In the 
time of Sir Apirana Ngata, he and an associate exhorted Māori to equip themselves for 
the material world of the Pākehā. As part of the preparation, the children of the time 
had to learn to speak English, along w ith other skills. That was appropriate for those 
times because the majority of Māori had but one language, the Māori language. In the 
light of that, we of New Zealand First do not think it right to call on the Crown to 
apologise for the actions of a great leader of the time. So what now? What fellow 
colleague Nanaia asserted is correct: we, the Māori Affairs Committee members, 
considered this matter and decided to refer it the Committee for consideration. That is 
the reason we are addressing that situation at this point in time. So that is our view on 
that matter. 
We heard the comments about the Te Mātāwai group, and at the time of my last 
address when this bill was in the House, I said to the Minister that we opposed a hapū 
register. It is not right that so  many tribes be crammed into five, four, or even three 
regions. I know this and so do you, Minister. 
Last week I also attended a meeting in the far north to speak on this matter about 
selecting a representative for the far north. The outcome was to delete the tribal names 
and and leave it as the far north region, and for the tribes in attendance at that meeting 
to select a representative for the region, as not all subtribes and tribes attended that 
meeting. If you don’t see your subtribe on the register, th en it might have been 
overlooked. That was the thinking of that meeting; that was the reasoning to dispense 
with those names. Leave it for that meeting to satisfy their wishes. 
So, Minister, despite the trials and tribulations in introducing this bill, we continue 
to commend you.
